ecac2845fd: Fighting games keep players through fairness; free-to-play games earn by selling advantage. Naruto's answer is to put “fairness” and “advantage” in different modes, then connect the two with ninjas.
cea531862e: “Do you own it” flows to the Arena; “how much do you have” flows to Ranked Points and PvE. The Arena only takes the ownership path, and progression stats are normalized there; Ranked Points and PvE only take the power path. Ninjas sit on both the acquisition line and the progression line, the only product that runs through both sides.
7ffbbd4f5c: Two flywheels meet at the ninja. The Arena flywheel is turned by new ninjas, and its spending comes in pulses; the power flywheel is turned by Ranked Points rewards, and its spending is continuous. The power flywheel reinforces itself, which is also why returning and new players struggle to catch up.
a534054321: Key numbers: a 25× gap for the same kind of product
fcdbf752c5: For the same outcome of getting one ninja, Premium Recruit converts to about ¥5,040 at top-up rates, while the Legend battle pass and direct coupon sales cost ¥198. The 25× gap shows Premium Recruit was never meant to be bought outright with cash.

708fa14961: Inference 1Gold is a “time currency”Gold has free sources; coupons come only from top-ups. Premium Recruit is how free players trade time for ninjas, and paying merely speeds it up. In the VIP shop the same item costs twice as much in gold as in coupons (350 vs. 175), so free gold does not undercut paid pricing.
3e3ac61325: Inference 2The high list price is a price anchorPremium Recruit's high converted cost makes a 1,980-coupon direct sale look like a bargain. The more certain an entry point is, the more it is priced in coupons; the 8 recruit entry points are tiered by certainty.
20c6506703: Inference 3The monthly card lines up with the battle passTopping up ¥50 a month yields 565 coupons, 2,260 over four months, just enough for one 1,980-coupon Legend battle pass. The pass season also lasts about 4 months, turning small payments into a fixed subscription.
6540c8c8f1: Inference 4Weekly limits cap heavy spendingBuying every weekly-limited item on the Power Deals page once adds up to about ¥600 a week. However rich a player is, that is all the material they can buy each week, which keeps top-end power growth under control.
1b0ed16b70: Scope: among the ¥198 channels, the battle pass grants an S-rank ninja while direct coupon sales are A-rank; the 300-pull figure for Premium Recruit is a player statistic, since the game only discloses the guaranteed S-rank shard per ten-pull. There are no official pay-rate or ARPPU figures, so those parts are inferred from mechanics, with no numbers claimed.
3140a04dd7: The spending ladder. The first three rungs are small, certain and subscription-like, aimed at raising the pay rate; the middle two are on-demand and repeatable, aimed at raising ARPPU; VIP accumulation sells nothing by itself and turns every earlier top-up into sunk cost. Prices are from the live game in October 2026.

f42f494021: Battlegrounds has no card collection: 8 players share one minion pool, and the result depends almost entirely on resource decisions inside a single match. This teardown looks only at the single match: where Gold comes from and how it is spent, how the minion pool limits choice, and how gaps in strength open up and are reined in. Based on Season 14, October 2026; I have played this mode for 501 hours, with a rating of 6,120.
90d406ee0f: Share of first-10-turn income spent on upgrades46%33 of 72 Gold
fc18567ace: A/B test sample size8,200matches per group, top proposal
73a9ddc9cd: All four findings rest on numbers. The four charts below are the most important calculations in the full text. Rules are taken from the live Season 14 game and official patch notes; the curves and shares are my own calculations.
838b6ceb76: Upgrades eat nearly half the income. On a sample curve that upgrades the Tavern every other turn, the first 10 turns bring in 72 Gold, of which 33 (46%) go to upgrades, leaving 0 to 2 Gold for minions on upgrade turns. The basic rhythm of a match is therefore one turn to upgrade, one turn to buy power, and players deviate from that baseline: upgrade back to back on high health, stay and roll on low health.
023d3bc4f2: Scarcity is guaranteed by copy counts. The shop draws only from the remaining copies, with no separate tier weights. A Tier 1 card has 15 copies and a triple takes 20%; a Tier 6 card has 7 copies and one triple takes 43%, so a second player can hardly make another.
eccfc085e6: What snowballs is the board, not the economy. With no interest and no win-streak bonus, the leader has the same budget each turn as everyone else; none of the four brakes weakens the leader directly, they only limit how fast an advantage grows.
1525a905b3: The damage cap holds back bursts on turns 4 to 10. In that stretch the theoretical maximum damage reaches 3.2× the cap. With 30 health and no armor, a capped player cannot be eliminated before turn 5; once the top 4 is reached the cap is lifted, and the final is settled in a turn or two.
27688b1b38: Payment only buys choice. The season pass widens the starting hero pick from 2 to 4, plus cosmetics, and sells no in-match stats. But heroes differ in strength, and two more options mean two more chances at a strong one: assuming 20% of heroes are strong in the current patch, the chance of seeing at least one is 1 − 0.8² = 36% with 2 options and 1 − 0.8⁴ = 59% with 4.
210d19d284: Compared with Naruto Mobile: Naruto's progression accumulates over months and years, and payment can buy progress directly; Battlegrounds compresses progression into one match, and payment barely touches in-match numbers. I never bought the pass and always picked from 2, yet still climbed above 6,000: paying raises the odds of getting a strong hero, but does not lock free players out of any rating bracket.
686e3ba2d8: The four proposals are ordered by benefit, cost and risk. First comes a three-level hint in the shop for remaining copies: it changes only the interface, touches no rules, and closes the information gap.

06a2d68607: Top proposal: a three-level hint for remaining copies
d9ebba7a71: The shared pool is the core mind game of Battlegrounds, yet how many copies of a card remain is known only to veterans who can keep count and to players running third-party add-ons. Opponents' tribes are public; remaining copies are not.
a208f12856: Each minion card in the shop gets a three-level marker: plentiful (≥ 60% left), low (30%–60%), scarce (< 30%). For a Tier 6 card with 7 copies that means ≥ 5, 3–4 and ≤ 2 copies.
258175b437: The hover details for minions in hand and on board show the same three levels, making it easy to judge whether a triple is still possible.
7bb1cda057: No exact numbers are shown and no odds or copy counts change. A little vagueness remains, so precise counting still pays off for veterans.

555cd5321b: Randomization unitBy match, not by playerAll 8 players in a match are in the treatment group or all in control, so no match has only half its players seeing the information.
843d6ffd20: Allocation and duration10% of matches, at least 2 weeksStratified by rating bracket with the same treatment share in each; avoid the first week of a season, when new mechanics make the data swing widely.
de5d7c792f: Sample sizeAbout 8,200 matches per groupAssuming a 30% baseline for the primary metric, a minimum detectable change of 2 percentage points, α = 0.05 and power 0.8: n ≈ 2 × (1.96 + 0.84)² × 0.3 × 0.7 ÷ 0.02². The baseline has to come from logs.
4f29a75cc1: Decision ruleThree outcomes, three actionsPrimary metric drops significantly and guardrails hold: full rollout. Effective only at low ratings: enable for low ratings only. No change in the primary metric: do not ship, since contested tribes are then mostly not an information problem.
4360ef1daa: Current Tavern upgrade costs are 5, 7, 8, 11, 11, with uneven steps. Suppose each tier cost a fixed +2 instead, which looks tidier. The analysis concludes it should not be changed.
38d7ec6d87: Tier 4 stops being cheap. Today Tier 4 costs only 1 more than Tier 3, the cheapest step relative to income, so mid-game everyone naturally pushes to Tier 4. With linear costs, upgrading to Tier 4 on turn 6 leaves just 1 Gold, pushing that milestone later.
aed7860a6f: The step before Tier 5 disappears. Today the jump from 8 to 11 between Tier 4 and Tier 5 is the largest increase, forcing a decision at Tier 4: stop and buy power, or keep upgrading. With linear costs that decision point is flattened.
694e7c7236: Tier 6 comes later and less often. Tavern tier counts toward damage, so fewer players reaching Tier 6 means lower late-game damage and possibly longer matches.
1016bf8ee2: Current costs are non-linear in order to create a pause around Tier 4. Before tuning a number, first look at what role it plays in the pacing.
